title: Sennacherib Prism
summary: A prism inscribed with Sennacherib's annals, including the campaign against Judah.
historical_context: The Taylor Prism is a Neo-Assyrian royal account produced about a decade after Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign in Judah. Lachish palace reliefs provide a distinct royal visual commemoration of the same campaign horizon.
ancient_near_east_context: Assyrian annals and palace reliefs are primary imperial self-presentations: they identify places, rulers, tribute, deportation, and victory claims while selecting and arranging events to magnify the king.
literary_context: The prism's annalistic victory rhetoric and the reliefs' visual conquest sequence should be compared with the distinct narrative and prophetic aims of 2 Kings 18-19 and Isaiah 36-37.
covenantal_significance: The Assyrian evidence anchors the campaign's political setting but cannot decide the biblical writers' theological explanation of Jerusalem's survival.
canonical_role: The prism and Lachish reliefs provide independent Assyrian perspectives on the 701 BCE campaign compared with Second Kings and Isaiah.

related_objects.notes: The prism is a Neo-Assyrian royal inscription.
Lachish was captured in the 701 BCE Judah campaign and prominently commemorated in Sennacherib's palace.
The relief cycle visually complements the annalistic prism.
The cultural-background cluster compares the annals with biblical tribute notices and Assyrian royal media.

interpretive_notes.note: Royal annals and palace reliefs are primary evidence for Assyrian claims and commemorative choices, not neutral transcripts of the entire campaign.
Sennacherib's failure to claim Jerusalem's capture is historically relevant but does not by itself prove the biblical account's theological explanation.

claims.claim: Sennacherib's annals describe his 701 BCE campaign in Judah, tribute from Hezekiah, and Hezekiah's confinement in Jerusalem.
claims.rationale: The royal inscription is a primary Assyrian witness to the campaign; translation details and historical synthesis still require comparison with other sources.
claims.notes: The annals do not say that Jerusalem was captured.

claims.claim: Sennacherib's palace reliefs depict the siege and capture of Lachish, captives, booty, and the enthroned Assyrian king within the 701 BCE Judah campaign.
claims.rationale: The labeled palace cycle and its archaeological context identify Lachish and a royal victory display; reconstruction details remain debated.
claims.notes: The relief is evidence for Assyrian commemoration of Lachish, not an image of Jerusalem's siege.

evidence_items.title: Taylor Prism account of Sennacherib's Judah campaign
evidence_items.description: A six-sided baked-clay prism inscribed in Akkadian with Sennacherib's royal annals, including his campaign against fortified Judahite cities and his treatment of Hezekiah.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The object, text, provenance history, and Neo-Assyrian date are well documented; historical use remains genre-sensitive because royal annals are self-presentation.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The inscription independently anchors Sennacherib, Hezekiah, Judah, tribute, and the 701 BCE campaign that frame 2 Kings 18-19 and Isaiah 36-37, while its different perspective prevents it from being treated as a neutral transcript of the biblical account.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The annals name Hezekiah of Judah, claim the capture of fortified Judahite towns, describe tribute, and portray Hezekiah as confined in Jerusalem; they do not claim Jerusalem's capture.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: The text is compared with Kings, Isaiah, Chronicles, other Assyrian inscriptions, and destruction evidence to reconstruct the campaign; harmonization details and rhetorical emphases remain debated.

temporal_scope.narrative_setting: Royal retrospective on the 701 BCE Judah campaign
temporal_scope.notes: Artifact date and recounted campaign date are intentionally distinguished.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: Both sources place Sennacherib's campaign against Judah and Hezekiah in the same historical horizon, while narrating it from different perspectives.
The annals' silence about capturing Jerusalem is relevant comparative evidence but does not itself establish the biblical account's explanation of the outcome.
The inscription supplies Assyrian royal context for the campaign narrated in Isaiah while retaining a distinct genre and viewpoint.

evidence_items.title: Lachish relief depiction of Sennacherib's Judah campaign
evidence_items.description: A palace relief cycle from Nineveh depicts Assyrian assault, captives, booty, and Sennacherib enthroned before Lachish.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The panels, palace provenance, Neo-Assyrian date, and Lachish identification are well documented; individual scene reconstruction remains genre- and context-sensitive.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The relief independently anchors Lachish as a major Assyrian victory in the campaign horizon of 2 Kings 18 and Isaiah 36, while its focus on a captured city contrasts with the prism's treatment of Jerusalem.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The surviving cycle shows a fortified city's assault and aftermath, deportees and booty, and Sennacherib receiving the presentation associated with Lachish.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: The cycle is read as a carefully designed royal victory display connected with the 701 BCE campaign; topographic, sequencing, and historical details are reconstructed in dialogue with the excavated site.
